_note: Batch 5 — workflow and technique. All 50, closing that bucket. These are about habits and order of operations rather than settings, which is why most of them have no params: the answer is a decision, not a number.

questions.q: How do I prepare a session before mixing?
questions.short: Name, colour, group and clean before you touch a fader. An hour here saves three later.
steps: Rename every track to what it is, not what the recording software called it.
Colour-code by family: drums, bass, vocals, instruments.
Route everything into buses before adding a single plugin.
Clean the obvious: dead space, counts, coughs, clicks.
Set a rough balance with faders only, and save that as a checkpoint.
questions.why: Mixing is a sequence of comparisons, and anything that slows a comparison down costs you attention you need for listening. A session you can navigate without thinking is the difference between making fifty decisions in an hour and making ten.
questions.watch: Preparation can become procrastination. An hour is enough; a day means you are avoiding the mix.

questions.q: What order should I mix in?
questions.short: Balance, then low end, then the lead, then everything else, then space. Repeat.
steps: Rough balance with faders only, no processing.
Get the kick and bass relationship right. Nothing works until that does.
Place the lead vocal next, at the level it will finish at.
Fit the rest around those three.
Add reverb and delay last, when the dry mix already works.
questions.why: Every element's treatment depends on what it is competing with, so settling the biggest relationships first means fewer decisions get invalidated later. Low end and lead vocal are the two that constrain everything else, which is why they come before anything you could call detail.
questions.watch: Adding reverb early makes every balance decision underneath it wrong, and you will not notice until the end.

questions.q: Should I start with the drums or the vocal?
questions.short: Whichever carries the song. In gospel and R&B start with the vocal; in afrobeats start with the groove.
steps: Ask what a listener would notice first if it were wrong. Start there.
Vocal-led genres: set the vocal, then build the track under it.
Groove-led genres: set the kick, bass and percussion, then fit the vocal in.
Either way, get that element to final quality before touching anything else.
Do not start with whatever is easiest. That is how mixes end up with no focus.
questions.why: The first element you mix becomes the reference everything else is judged against, so it should be the one the song is about. Starting with drums on a ballad produces a mix with excellent drums and a vocal squeezed into what is left.
questions.watch: The drums-first habit comes from rock engineering. It is a convention, not a rule.

questions.q: How long should a mix take?
aliases: how long to mix a song
questions.short: Four to eight hours for a professional mix, across two sessions. Longer usually means worse.
steps: Aim to get 80% of the way in the first two hours.
Stop at four hours whether it is finished or not.
Sleep, then spend one to two hours the next day on the remaining 20%.
If you are on hour ten, you are no longer improving it.
Track your time for a few mixes — most people are slower than they think and better than they fear.
questions.why: Mix quality rises quickly and then plateaus, while ear fatigue rises steadily. The crossover is usually around four hours, after which each additional hour is more likely to make the mix worse than better.
questions.watch: Speed comes from preparation and decisiveness, not from working faster. Rushing the prep costs more time than it saves.

questions.q: When should I take a break?
questions.short: Every 45–60 minutes, for ten minutes of actual silence. Not a different loud thing.
steps: Break every 45–60 minutes.
Make it silent — no music, no video, no headphones.
Ten minutes is enough for most of your high-frequency sensitivity to recover.
Break immediately if you catch yourself making a move you already made an hour ago.
Take the longest break before the final decisions, not after them.
questions.why: Temporary threshold shift from sustained exposure is strongest in the 2–6 kHz region and recovers substantially within minutes of quiet. Putting on a podcast during a break prevents that recovery, which is why the silence matters more than the duration.
questions.watch: The moment you most feel like pushing through is usually the moment the break is most needed.

questions.q: How do I set up a mix template?
questions.short: Buses, sends and routing — not plugins. A template of settings is a template of wrong settings.
steps: Create your standard buses: drums, bass, vocals, instruments, mix bus.
Create two or three reverb sends and one delay send, all set up and filtered.
Add a metering plugin and a reference track slot on the master.
Leave the channel strips empty. Every song needs different processing.
Save it, use it for three mixes, then revise it.
questions.why: Routing is the part that is identical between songs, so templating it saves setup time without presuming anything about the music. Templated channel plugins presume what the source sounds like, which is exactly the thing you have not heard yet.
questions.watch: A template with thirty tracks of plugins you never bypass makes every one of your mixes sound the same.

questions.q: How do I name and colour tracks usefully?
questions.short: Name by role, not by source. Colour by family. Both should work at a glance from across the room.
steps: Name by what it does: LEAD VOX, VOX DBL L, not Audio 14.
Prefix groups so they sort together: DRM KICK, DRM SNR, VOX LEAD.
Colour by family and keep the same colours across every project.
Mark anything muted or parked with a distinct colour so you do not forget it.
Rename as you go. Renaming at the end never happens.
questions.why: You navigate a session hundreds of times in a mix, and every moment spent working out which track is which is attention taken from listening. Consistent colours across projects also mean you can read a session you have not opened in a year.
questions.watch: Over-elaborate naming schemes get abandoned mid-session, which is worse than none.

questions.q: What is a rough balance and why does it matter so much?
questions.short: The whole song balanced with faders alone. If it does not work here, no plugin will save it.
steps: Set every fader by ear with no processing at all. Twenty minutes, not two hours.
Play the loudest section and the quietest and make the balance work for both.
Stop when you can hear every part and the song makes sense.
Save it. Everything after this is refinement, and you may want to come back.
If it does not work, the problem is the arrangement, not the mix.
questions.why: Most of what a listener experiences as a good mix is relative level. Processing refines the balance and makes it hold up under movement, but it cannot create one — which is why a mix that was wrong at this stage stays wrong however many plugins are added.
questions.watch: If one fader has to be at the top or bottom of its travel, fix the clip gain instead.

questions.q: Should I use the fader or the clip gain?
questions.short: Clip gain for consistency within a track, fader for the balance between tracks.
steps: Use clip gain to level phrases, notes and sections against each other.
Use the fader to set where that evened-out track sits against everything else.
Do all clip gain before any processing, so plugins see a consistent input.
Keep faders near unity so you can see the balance at a glance.
questions.why: Clip gain happens before the channel's plugins, so it changes what the compressor and saturator receive. The fader happens after, so it changes only the output. Using the fader to fix an inconsistent performance means the compressor is still reacting to the inconsistency.
questions.watch: Clip gain on a noisy recording raises the noise with the quiet parts. Clean first.

questions.q: When do I commit and when do I stay flexible?
questions.short: Commit to anything that is part of the sound. Stay flexible on anything that is a balance decision.
steps: Commit: amp sims, creative effects, tuning, time editing, anything with a long render.
Stay flexible: level, EQ, compression, reverb sends.
Always keep the unprocessed file alongside the committed one.
Commit earlier on a long project and later on a short one.
If a plugin choice is slowing the session down, commit it and move on.
questions.why: Unlimited flexibility is a cost, not a benefit: every open decision is one you have to make again on every pass. Committing the choices that define the sound removes them from consideration and leaves attention for the ones that genuinely need revisiting.
questions.watch: Committing without keeping the original is how a revision request becomes a re-record.

questions.q: How should I organise my buses?
questions.short: One per family, all into the mix bus. Five or six buses, not fifteen.
steps: Drums, bass, lead vocal, backing vocals, instruments, effects returns.
Route every channel into one of them; nothing goes straight to the master.
Put family-wide processing on the bus, not repeated on each channel.
Add a parallel bus for drums and one for vocals if you use parallel compression.
Keep the structure the same across projects so you can work without thinking.
questions.why: Buses let you treat a family as one thing, which is both faster and more coherent than treating eight channels individually. They also give you a single fader for the relationship that matters most — drums against vocals against everything else.
questions.watch: Too many buses recreates the problem they solve. If a bus has one channel in it, it is not a bus.

questions.q: VCA or group — what is the difference and when do I use each?
questions.short: A group routes audio and can be processed. A VCA only moves faders and changes nothing else.
steps: Use a group when you want to process the family together — EQ, compression, saturation.
Use a VCA when you only want to change levels without affecting bus compression or sends.
Use a VCA over a drum group so riding the drums does not change how the bus compressor behaves.
Use both: group for processing, VCA over it for riding.
questions.why: Lowering a group fader reduces the signal going into anything after it, including the master bus compressor and any post-fader sends. A VCA moves the member channels' faders instead, so the relationship between the source and its own processing stays intact.
questions.watch: Pre-fader sends ignore VCA moves entirely. Check which kind your reverb sends are.

questions.q: How do I mix on headphones only?
questions.short: Entirely possible. Use one pair you know well, check in mono often, and trust meters for low end.
steps: Use one pair as your reference and learn them over months rather than switching.
Check mono frequently — headphones hide phase problems that speakers expose.
Use a spectrum analyser for low-end decisions; most headphones mislead below 60 Hz.
Reference commercial tracks constantly, at matched loudness.
Check on a phone speaker and in a car before calling it finished.
questions.why: Headphones remove the room entirely, which is an advantage in an untreated space. The costs are an unnatural stereo image — each ear hears only one channel — and low-frequency response that varies enormously between models and even between fittings.
questions.watch: Headphone width always flatters. A mix that feels nicely wide on headphones is usually too wide.

questions.q: How do I calibrate my monitors?
questions.short: Set one repeatable level with pink noise and a meter, mark the knob, and stop moving it.
steps: Play pink noise at −20 dBFS through one speaker.
Measure at the listening position with an SPL meter set to C-weighting, slow.
Adjust until it reads 79 dB SPL for a small room, then repeat for the other speaker.
Mark that position on the monitor controller and treat it as your reference.
Position the speakers and your head as an equilateral triangle, tweeters at ear height.
questions.why: Because frequency perception changes with level, a repeatable monitoring level is what makes your judgements comparable from session to session. Calibration is not about a magic number — it is about always being at the same one.
questions.watch: Calibration does not fix a room. An uncalibrated treated room beats a calibrated untreated one.

questions.q: How do I treat a bedroom for mixing?
questions.short: Bass traps in the corners first, then first reflection points. Foam squares on the wall do almost nothing.
steps: Put thick absorption in the vertical corners. Low frequencies are the whole problem in a small room.
Treat the first reflection points on the side walls, found with a mirror and a friend.
Treat the ceiling above the listening position if you can.
Sit at 38% of the room's length from the front wall, facing the short wall.
Keep speakers at least 20 cm from the wall behind them, or follow their manual.
questions.why: A small room's dominant problem is modal buildup below about 300 Hz, where wavelengths are comparable to the room's dimensions. Thin foam absorbs only high frequencies, so it makes a room sound dead and leaves every low-end problem exactly where it was.
questions.watch: Treating only the high end makes mixes that are too bright, because the room no longer gives you any.

questions.q: How do I test a mix in the car?
questions.short: Low end and vocal level, nothing else. Play a reference immediately before and after.
steps: Bring a reference track and play it first so your ears adjust to the car.
Listen for two things: is the low end out of control, and is the vocal the right level.
Ignore stereo width and fine tonal balance — a car gets both wrong.
Drive somewhere; stationary with the engine off is not how anyone listens.
Note the problems, fix them in the studio, and do not mix in the car.
questions.why: Cars have a strong resonant boost around 60–120 Hz from the cabin, so low-end problems that are inaudible on small monitors become obvious. That exaggeration is what makes a car useful for one specific check and misleading for every other.
questions.watch: Every car is different. Use the same car every time or the test tells you nothing.

questions.q: How do I test a mix on a phone speaker?
questions.short: Ask one question: can you hear the bass line and the vocal. Nothing else is testable there.
steps: Play it on the phone's own speaker, not through earbuds.
Listen for whether the bass line's melody is followable.
Listen for whether the vocal sits above everything.
If the bass is missing, add harmonics with saturation rather than low end.
Ignore everything about the low end itself — the speaker cannot reproduce it.
questions.why: A phone speaker rolls off steeply below about 400 Hz and has a strong mid-range peak, so it is effectively a test of your 400 Hz to 4 kHz balance. That happens to be where intelligibility and the implied bass line both live, which makes it the most informative two-minute check available.
questions.watch: Do not fix a phone-speaker problem with EQ on the master. Fix it on the source that failed.

questions.q: How do I handle client revision notes?
questions.short: Translate the feeling into a parameter before you touch anything, and confirm you understood.
steps: Collect all notes before making any change. Piecemeal revisions undo each other.
Translate each one: 'more energy' might mean the drums, the vocal, or the arrangement — ask.
Ask for a timestamp and a reference for anything vague.
Make every change, then listen to the whole song once before sending.
Keep the previous version. Clients change their minds and you will need it.
questions.why: Clients describe outcomes and engineers work in parameters, so almost every revision request needs translating before it can be acted on. Guessing the translation is how three rounds of revisions become eight.
questions.watch: Doing a revision you disagree with without saying so is worse than saying so and then doing it.

questions.q: How do I deliver stems?
questions.short: Same start point, same sample rate, no master processing, named clearly.
steps: Export every stem from bar one, even if the part starts later. They must line up on drop-in.
Keep the session's sample rate and bit depth; export 24-bit minimum.
Bypass the mix bus chain, or supply both versions and label which is which.
Group sensibly: drums, bass, vocals, backing vocals, instruments, effects.
Name them with the song title, the stem name and the tempo.
questions.why: Stems exist so someone else can rebalance without the session, which only works if they drop in at the same position and sum back to something close to your mix. A stem that starts where its audio starts is the single most common reason that fails.
questions.watch: Stems that include the mix bus compressor will not sum back to your mix when recombined.

questions.q: What exactly do I send to a mastering engineer?
questions.short: One 24-bit WAV at session rate, peaking around −6 dBFS, limiter off, no dither.
steps: Bounce 24-bit or 32-bit float WAV at the session's sample rate. Never MP3.
Leave the mix bus limiter off. Keep any compression that is part of the sound.
Peak around −6 dBFS. The exact number matters less than not clipping.
Do not dither.
Include a reference track, any notes, and the song's intended order if it is an album.
questions.why: A mastering engineer needs room to work and a mix that has not already been pushed against a ceiling. The limiter is the one thing that removes both the headroom and the information they would use, which is why it comes off even when it sounded good.
questions.watch: If you mixed into a limiter and it is part of the sound, say so and send both versions.

questions.q: How do I make an instrumental and a TV mix?
questions.short: Instrumental has no vocals at all. A TV mix keeps the backing vocals and loses only the lead.
steps: Instrumental: mute the lead, all doubles, harmonies and ad-libs.
TV mix: mute only the lead and its doubles; keep the backing vocals and choir.
Keep every other level identical — do not rebalance to fill the gap.
Export both at the same loudness as the main mix.
Name them clearly: Title (Instrumental), Title (TV Mix).
questions.why: A TV mix exists so an artist can perform the lead live over the record, which means everything except their part must be exactly as released. Rebalancing to fill the hole makes the two versions sound like different mixes the moment the artist starts singing.
questions.watch: Check for lead vocal bleed in the reverb returns. Vocal reverb left in an instrumental is a common slip.

questions.q: How do I make a radio edit?
questions.short: Mute, reverse or replace — do not bleep unless asked. Keep the breath and the timing.
steps: Mute the word on the lead and all its doubles and ad-libs at once.
Check the reverb and delay returns; the word often survives in the tail.
Keep the surrounding breath so the edit does not sound like a dropout.
Reversing or pitching the word is usually less distracting than a bleep.
Shorten long intros and outros if the brief asks for a time limit.
questions.why: A clean edit works when the listener does not notice it happened, and what gives most edits away is not the missing word but the missing room — the sudden absence of breath and reverb that was there a syllable earlier.
questions.watch: Muting on the lead alone leaves the word audible on the doubles. Mute the whole vocal group.

questions.q: How do I version and back up a mix?
questions.short: Save a new version at every milestone, keep three copies in two places, and never overwrite.
steps: Save a new session version at every meaningful stage: rough, v1, v2, client, final.
Date the filename. Song_Mix_v3_2026-02-14 beats Song_Mix_FINAL_real.
Keep three copies: working drive, local backup, cloud.
Bounce a reference MP3 with every version so you can hear old ones without opening them.
Never overwrite a version a client has heard.
questions.why: Mixing is non-linear and you will want to go back. More importantly, a client who approved v4 and now wants 'the one from last week' is asking for a file you either have or do not — and reconstructing it from memory is not possible.
questions.watch: A backup on the same physical drive is not a backup.

questions.q: How do I recall an old mix?
questions.short: Open the bounced reference first and compare. Missing plugins are the usual failure.
steps: Play the bounced reference from that version before opening the session.
Open the session and compare the playback to the bounce immediately.
If they differ, the usual cause is a missing or updated plugin — check for bypassed slots.
Keep an audio print of each stem if the mix matters enough to recall reliably.
For anything commercially important, archive printed stems rather than relying on the session.
questions.why: A session is a set of instructions that depend on software that changes. Printed audio depends on nothing, which is why archives that matter are printed rather than saved.
questions.watch: Plugin updates change how presets sound. Matching version numbers matters more than most people expect.

questions.q: How do I collaborate on a mix remotely?
questions.short: Agree the sample rate and the tempo map first, then exchange stems from bar one.
steps: Agree sample rate, bit depth and tempo before anyone records anything.
Exchange consolidated stems from bar one, never session files, unless you share a DAW and plugins.
Include a rough mix MP3 with every delivery so there is a shared reference.
Use timestamped notes for feedback, not adjectives.
Keep one person as the owner of the master session.
questions.why: Almost every remote mixing problem is a mismatch agreed too late: a different sample rate, a different tempo, a file that starts at the wrong place. Settling those three before any audio moves removes most of the friction.
questions.watch: Two people both editing the master session is how a project loses a day's work.

questions.q: How do I comp a vocal from many takes?
questions.short: Comp for emotion first, pitch second, and cut on breaths rather than on words.
steps: Listen through every take once without editing, marking the moments that move you.
Build the comp phrase by phrase, choosing feel over technical accuracy.
Cut on breaths or in silence; never in the middle of a sustained note.
Crossfade every edit, even the ones that sound clean.
Listen to the finished comp straight through — it must sound like one performance.
questions.why: A comp assembled from the most accurate fragments usually sounds like an assembly. Listeners respond to conviction and continuity, both of which live in phrasing across a whole line rather than in individual notes.
questions.watch: Comping at the word level produces vocals that are technically perfect and emotionally flat.

questions.q: How do I tune a vocal without it sounding fake?
questions.short: Correct the centre of notes and leave the transitions alone. Slides and scoops are the performance.
steps: Use graphical mode and fix individual notes rather than applying global correction.
Correct the sustained centre of a note and leave its start and end untouched.
Keep vibrato. Flattening it is the fastest route to a synthetic vocal.
Fix only the notes that are actually wrong — usually four or five in a verse.
Listen to the corrected take against the original at matched level before accepting it.
questions.why: The ear identifies a voice as human partly through its pitch instability: the scoop into a note, the drift across a long one, the vibrato. Correction that removes those removes the cues, which is why a perfectly in-tune vocal can sound less real than a slightly flat one.
questions.watch: Over-tuning is almost always done while soloed. Check it in the mix before deciding it is too much.

questions.q: How do I time-align a doubled vocal?
questions.short: Align the consonants and leave the vowels. The ear only hears timing at the edges.
steps: Zoom to the consonants and drag each double so its hard consonants match the lead.
Leave the vowels wherever they fall; that difference is what makes doubles thick.
Pay most attention to word endings — a late 'T' or 'S' is the most audible flam.
Do not quantise to a grid. Align to the lead take.
Check in mono; alignment problems show up as thinning.
questions.why: The ear detects timing differences at transients, so a vowel drifting five milliseconds is inaudible while a consonant doing the same is a flam. Aligning everything removes the small differences that create width.
questions.watch: Perfectly aligned doubles fuse into the lead and stop being doubles at all.

questions.q: How do I edit drum timing without killing the feel?
questions.short: Fix the hits that are wrong, not the ones that are early. Groove is consistent offset; sloppiness is random.
steps: Listen first and mark only the hits that sound wrong, not the ones the grid disagrees with.
Check whether the drummer is consistently ahead or behind — that is the feel, leave it.
If you quantise, use 50–80% strength, never 100%.
Move the whole kit together, so the close mics and overheads stay phase-aligned.
Compare to the unedited version before accepting.
questions.why: A drummer consistently 15 ms behind the grid is playing a laid-back feel, and the grid is the thing that is wrong. Random variation is sloppiness. The distinction is consistency, and only listening reveals it.
questions.watch: Quantising one mic and not the others destroys the phase relationship across the kit.

questions.q: How do I replace a bad snare?
questions.short: Blend a sample under the original rather than replacing it, and match the room before the tone.
steps: Trigger a sample from the original hit rather than deleting the original track.
Blend the sample under the live snare at 20–50% — full replacement loses the ghost notes.
Match the sample's room to the kit's, or use a dry sample and share the kit's reverb.
Check the timing of the trigger; even 3 ms late sounds like a flam.
Keep the original overheads untouched. They still have the real snare in them.
questions.why: The overheads and room mics contain the original snare whether you like it or not, so a full replacement puts two different snares in the mix. Blending underneath adds what the original lacked while the ensemble stays coherent.
questions.watch: Triggers miss ghost notes and fire on bleed. Check the whole song, not the first chorus.

questions.q: How do I layer two kick samples?
questions.short: One for the sub, one for the click, filtered so they never overlap, and phase-aligned.
steps: Pick one sample for the low end and low-pass it at 120 Hz.
Pick one for the attack and high-pass it at 150–200 Hz.
Align their transients exactly; even 2 ms apart sounds like two kicks.
Check polarity — if the layered kick is thinner than either alone, flip one.
Bus them and process the bus, not the individual layers.
questions.why: Two full-range kicks summed produce comb filtering wherever their phase disagrees, which is why a layered kick often sounds weaker than either sample alone. Filtering each to its own job removes the overlap and therefore removes the cancellation.
questions.watch: Check the layered kick in mono and on a phone. Phase problems hide on big speakers.

questions.q: How do I build a vocal chain from scratch?
questions.short: Clean, control, shape, colour, place. Add one stage at a time and only if the previous one left a problem.
steps: Clean: high-pass, remove noise, de-ess lightly, fix clicks.
Control: compressor one, slow and gentle, 3 dB.
Shape: subtractive EQ for resonances, then compressor two, fast, 3 dB.
Colour: saturation, then additive EQ for presence and air.
Place: de-ess again, then reverb and delay on sends.
Add each stage only if the one before left something unsolved.
questions.why: Each stage changes what the next one receives, so an order that cleans before it controls and controls before it colours means every processor is working on a signal it can handle. Chains assembled from a preset usually have stages solving problems that no longer exist.
questions.watch: A chain built because it is the standard chain will have plugins in it doing nothing. Bypass each and check.

questions.q: In what order should vocal plugins go?
questions.short: High-pass, de-ess, compress, EQ, saturate, de-ess again, then sends. The second de-esser is the trick.
steps: High-pass first so the compressor does not react to rumble.
Light de-esser before the compressor, so it does not amplify the esses.
Compressor, then subtractive EQ, then a second compressor if needed.
Saturation and additive EQ after the dynamics are settled.
Second de-esser last, because the saturation and air shelf brought the esses back.
Reverb and delay on sends, never as inserts.
questions.why: Every brightening stage raises sibilance, so a single de-esser placed early is undone by everything after it and one placed late has to work twice as hard. Splitting it across the chain is the single change that most improves a vocal chain.
questions.watch: This is a sensible default, not a rule. Saturation before compression is a valid and different sound.

questions.q: How do I save and reuse a vocal chain across songs?
questions.short: Save the structure with every plugin at neutral, not the settings. Settings are about one singer.
steps: Save the chain with the plugins loaded and every control at a neutral starting point.
Keep the order and the routing; discard the values.
Note the intent of each stage in the preset name so you remember why it is there.
Re-set the threshold and frequency for every new voice; those never transfer.
Revise the saved chain every few months as your habits change.
questions.why: What transfers between songs is the order of operations, which reflects how signal flow works. What does not transfer is every frequency and threshold, because those describe one singer in one room on one microphone.
questions.watch: A chain preset with settings intact is why engineers end up with twenty mixes that sound the same.

questions.q: How do I gain stage a chain of plugins?
questions.short: Match output to input at every stage so bypassing a plugin does not change the level.
steps: Set the channel to peak around −12 dBFS before any plugin.
After each plugin, adjust its output so bypassing it does not change the loudness.
Check the level between every stage, not only at the end.
Use a gain plugin between stages if a processor has no output control.
Re-check after any change to a plugin earlier in the chain.
questions.why: Analogue-modelled plugins behave differently at different input levels, so an uncontrolled gain structure means each plugin is operating somewhere you did not choose. Matched gain also makes every bypass comparison honest, which is the only way to tell whether a plugin is helping.
questions.watch: Level creeping up through a chain makes every stage sound like an improvement when only the gain changed.

questions.q: How do I clean up a noisy recording?
questions.short: Edit the silence out first, then de-noise gently. Most noise problems are solved by muting.
steps: Cut or gate the gaps between phrases. That removes most of the perceived noise immediately.
Use a de-noiser at the lightest setting that works — 4–6 dB of reduction, not 20.
High-pass and low-pass to the useful range of the source before de-noising.
Expect artefacts: de-noising trades noise for a watery quality, and too much is worse than hiss.
Check the quietest passage, which is where the processing shows.
questions.why: Noise is only perceptible where there is no signal masking it, so removing the gaps removes most of the problem without touching the recording. De-noising the signal itself always costs something, which is why it should be the last and lightest step.
questions.watch: Heavy de-noising on a vocal removes breath and air along with the hiss, and both are the performance.

questions.q: How do I remove a hum or buzz?
questions.short: Notch the fundamental and its harmonics. 50 Hz in most of the world, 60 Hz in the Americas.
steps: Identify the fundamental: 50 Hz or 60 Hz depending on your mains supply.
Notch it with a very narrow Q of 20 or higher, and notch its harmonics too.
Use a dedicated hum remover if the buzz has many harmonics; manual notching gets tedious.
A high-pass alone will not work — the harmonics reach well into the mid-range.
Fix the cause next time: a ground loop, an unbalanced cable, or a dimmer on the same circuit.
questions.why: Mains hum is a periodic signal, so its energy sits at the supply frequency and exact multiples of it rather than spread across a band. That makes it one of the few problems a very narrow notch genuinely solves, because the notch can be narrower than anything musical.
questions.watch: Notching at 50 Hz also notches any bass note at 50 Hz. Check the bass line through the filter.

questions.q: How do I deal with a room that is audible on every mic?
questions.short: Lean into it rather than fighting it. Match everything to that room instead of removing it from each source.
steps: Find the room's resonance by sweeping between 200 and 800 Hz on the most exposed source.
Cut it once on the mix bus rather than on every channel.
Add a reverb that matches the room's character to the sources that lack it.
Gate or expand only the most percussive sources, and gently.
Accept it. A consistent room is a sound; an inconsistently removed room is a mess.
questions.why: When every microphone captured the same room, the room is effectively part of the recording's identity. Removing it from some sources and not others destroys the coherence that made it sound like a band playing together, which is usually worse than the room itself.
questions.watch: De-reverb plugins on a whole band produce artefacts faster than they produce clarity.

questions.q: How do I fade in and out cleanly?
questions.short: Fade at zero crossings, use short crossfades on every edit, and fade out over at least two bars.
steps: Put a short fade — 5–20 ms — on the start and end of every clip. This removes clicks.
Crossfade every edit, even ones that sound clean.
For a song fade-out, use at least two bars and an exponential curve, not linear.
Start the fade on a downbeat and end it in silence, not mid-note.
Check the fade on headphones; clicks hide on speakers.
questions.why: A click is a discontinuity in the waveform, which happens whenever audio starts or stops at a non-zero value. A fade of even a few milliseconds removes the discontinuity, which is why the fix is so short and so reliable.
questions.watch: Linear fade-outs sound like someone turning a knob. Exponential matches how the ear perceives level.

questions.q: How do I automate a mix instead of setting and forgetting?
questions.short: Automate after the static mix works, section by section, starting with the vocal.
steps: Finish the static balance first. Automation refines; it cannot rescue.
Start with the lead vocal, phrase by phrase.
Then automate section-level changes: verse to chorus, builds, drops.
Then automate effects — sends up on the last word of a line, down during it.
Listen to the whole song in one pass after each stage.
questions.why: A static mix is a single compromise that has to serve every section, and no single balance serves a quiet verse and a full chorus. Automation is how a mix stops being an average and starts following the arrangement.
questions.watch: Automating before the static mix works means redoing all of it when the balance changes.

questions.q: How do I ride a vocal fader?
questions.short: Phrase by phrase, by small amounts, until every word is audible without the compressor working harder.
steps: Play the song and write fader moves in real time for a first pass.
Then refine phrase by phrase, in 0.5–1 dB steps.
Ride up for quiet words and down for shouted ones, not the reverse.
Ride before the compressor with clip gain for big corrections, after it with the fader for fine ones.
Aim for every word to be equally intelligible, not equally loud.
questions.why: A compressor reacts to amplitude while a listener responds to intelligibility, and a word can be loud and unclear or quiet and perfectly audible. Riding is how you fix the second thing, which is why it achieves what more compression never does.
questions.watch: Riding with the fader after heavy compression fights the compressor. Fix the big moves with clip gain.

questions.q: How do I automate effects rather than instruments?
questions.short: Ride the sends, not the returns. Up on the last word of a line, down during the words.
steps: Automate the send level, so the effect follows the performance rather than the fader.
Push the reverb or delay up on the final word of a phrase and down during the next.
Open the reverb at section changes, then close it again.
Automate the return's filter for a sense of the space changing.
Mute the effects entirely for one section if the arrangement needs the contrast.
questions.why: A static send has to be low enough to keep the words clear, which means it is too low to create any sense of space. Automating it gives you both: dry and intelligible during the line, wet and large in the gaps.
questions.watch: Automating the return instead of the send changes the level of every source using that reverb.

questions.q: How do I know a mix is finished?
aliases: how do I know when to stop
questions.short: When your changes stop making it better and start making it different. Check with fresh ears.
steps: Sleep on it. The first thirty seconds of the next morning's listen is the most honest test.
Play it on three systems. If no problem recurs, it is done.
Notice whether your last five moves were improvements or alternatives.
Ask whether the song moves you. If it does, stop.
Set a deadline before you start. Mixes expand to fill the time available.
questions.why: There is no objective finish line, so the practical test is whether you are still reducing problems or just exploring options. Once the changes are lateral rather than upward, more time is spending attention without buying quality.
questions.watch: The urge to keep going is usually anxiety about the song, not a problem with the mix.

questions.q: How do I stop endlessly tweaking?
questions.short: Set a deadline, keep a list instead of acting on every thought, and bounce versions.
steps: Set a finish time before you start and honour it.
When you notice something, write it on a list instead of fixing it immediately.
Fix the whole list in one pass, then listen once and stop.
Bounce a version at every milestone so going back is cheap and stopping is safe.
If you have made the same decision twice in opposite directions, it does not matter.
questions.why: Endless tweaking is usually driven by the fact that each small change is audible in isolation, which feels like progress. Batching the changes and judging them together restores the only scale that matters: whether the whole record is better.
questions.watch: A mix you are bored of is not a bad mix. Boredom is a consequence of hearing it two hundred times.

questions.q: How do I mix fast for a deadline?
questions.short: Spend the first twenty minutes on balance and the rest on the three things that matter most.
steps: Twenty minutes on a fader-only balance. Do not skip this; it is what makes the rest fast.
Pick the three biggest problems and fix only those.
Use buses: one EQ move on the drum bus beats eight on channels.
Automate the vocal and nothing else.
Bounce, listen once on a phone, fix anything fatal, send.
questions.why: Under time pressure the balance is worth more than every other decision combined, because it is what the listener experiences most directly. Skipping it to start processing is the most common way a rushed mix ends up both late and bad.
questions.watch: Fast does not mean skipping the phone check. That is the one test that catches fatal mistakes.

questions.q: How do I mix a song I did not record?
aliases: mix a song I didnt record
questions.short: Listen to the rough mix first and respect it. It contains the artist's intention.
steps: Listen to the rough mix twice before opening the session, and note what it gets right.
Ask what the artist likes about the rough. That tells you what not to change.
Find out what is missing and what is a placeholder before you start fixing things.
Fix the recording's real problems; do not reimagine the production.
Send your first version alongside the rough so the comparison is explicit.
questions.why: A rough mix made by whoever recorded it encodes decisions about what the song is, even when it is technically poor. Mixing without listening to it is how an engineer delivers something excellent that the artist does not recognise.
questions.watch: A rough mix that an artist has lived with for months is very hard to beat emotionally. Expect that.

questions.q: How do I take over someone else's session file?
questions.short: Save a copy, bypass everything, and rebuild from the raw tracks rather than untangling.
steps: Save a copy immediately and never work in the original.
Bounce their mix as a reference before you change anything.
Bypass every plugin and listen to the raw tracks.
Rebuild your own routing rather than reverse-engineering theirs.
Keep anything that is clearly a creative choice; discard anything that is just processing.
questions.why: Untangling someone else's chain takes longer than rebuilding and leaves you with decisions you do not understand. Starting from the raw tracks means every plugin in the final session is there because you put it there.
questions.watch: Missing plugins will silently change the session's sound. Check for inactive slots before judging anything.

questions.q: How do I set the same reference level in every session?
questions.short: Calibrate once, mark the knob, and treat that position as the only one you make decisions at.
steps: Calibrate with pink noise and an SPL meter, once.
Mark the position physically on the monitor controller.
Return to that mark whenever you are making a tonal decision.
Use other levels freely for checking, never for deciding.
Re-calibrate if you move the speakers or change the room.
questions.why: Your sense of what a correct balance sounds like is learned at a particular level, so changing the level changes the target. Keeping one reference position is what lets experience accumulate instead of resetting each session.
questions.watch: Headphone users need the same discipline. Find one comfortable volume and mark it in your interface.

questions.q: How do I keep mixes consistent across an album?
questions.short: Mix them in one period, use the same template, and compare every song against the first one you finished.
steps: Mix the whole project in as short a span as you can; your taste drifts over months.
Pick the strongest song, finish it, and make it the reference for all the others.
Use the same template, the same buses and the same reverbs across every song.
At the end, play all the songs back to back and fix only what stands out.
Leave final loudness matching to mastering; focus on tonal and spatial consistency.
questions.why: Consistency across a record is mostly about shared spaces and a shared tonal centre, both of which come free if the same reverbs and the same monitoring are used throughout. What breaks it is mixing over a long period, during which both your ears and your preferences move.
questions.watch: Consistent does not mean identical. A ballad and an uptempo song should not have the same balance.

questions.q: How do I archive a project properly?
questions.short: Consolidate audio, print stems, save a PDF of the session, and keep it in two places.
steps: Consolidate every track from bar one so the session does not depend on external files.
Print stems and a final mix as 24-bit WAV, and store them beside the session.
Save a screenshot or PDF of the mixer and the plugin list.
Include the rough mix, references and any client notes.
Store two copies in two physical locations. Verify you can open one.
questions.why: A session depends on a DAW version, plugin versions and licences that may not exist in five years. Printed audio depends on nothing, which is why a real archive contains both and the printed audio is the part that will survive.
questions.watch: An archive you have never tested restoring is not an archive. Open one, once, to check.
